Such thoughts in the breast of a man, so honest in conviction, so resolute in will, and so fearless in execution, was no barren sentiment ; and he deliberately determined to devote the rest of his life to the liberation of his country, arid the recovery of his own dignity þÿ of measuring the latter by a far higher standard than the vulgar one of rank, military distinction, power, or court favour. Resigning his seat as a Senator, lie insisted with Espartero on being allowed to return to Havannah þÿ a permission which he did not obtain without extreme difficulty, nor until after long resistance on the part of the Regent, it being contrary to the jealous policy of Spain, in the government of her rich colony, the Queen of Antilles, to allow an American born officer of rank or importance to go

tero, the noble head of the Liberal or Progressive party in Spain, alone made practicable the importunity with which Genetal j Lopez usisted on the demand, which he even enforced by making it the alternative to a resignation of his commission ; and it cannot ; respeet be denied that his own determined purpose m going, and the consequences which have resulted from it, proved clearly enough the policy of that rule, on the part of the Spanish Government, to which he thus succeeded in ' ausing himself to be made the fatal exception. It may be added that Lopez's secret wishes and views, early adopted, have made him an object of at least so much suspicion, in reference to Cuba, that several years before, by a proceeding emanating from Havannah, and from Tacon, then Captain-General, he had been subjected to a formal tiial on a charge of conspiring for the independence ol that colony, and having, at a dinner, proposed as a toast a sentiment to that effect. He succeeded, however, in baffling Ins enemies, and was acquitted. It was, we believe, in 1839 that he returned to (Juba. During the period ot the Captain-Generalship of Valdez, honour, friendship, and gratitude combined to require him to postpone any steps towards the accomplishment of that great purpose which never slept within his breast. The downfall of Espartcro, and the restoration of Maria Christina to power, supported by Narvaez and the army, by causing the recall of the virtuous Valdez (who was succeeded by O'Donnell, the predecessor of Roncall), re-

leased him from the personal obligations by which at lirst he had felt himself fettered ; and his friends in Havannah were surprised at the evident content and cheerfulness with which he received a change of parties, necessarily depriving him of the posis which he field in the military government of the island. Under Valdez he was Governor of Trinidad and Communder-in-Cliief of the Central Department, as well as President of the Military Com mission. He gladly laid down these posts on the arrival of the period oppoi- of tunity and freedom, for which he had impatiently waited ; and creating a pretext for remrning to the Central Department, in retirement (retaining, of course, his position and rank as General, though not on duty), by undertaking the working of an abandoned onper mine, he devoted himself mainly to

8 sr» <8 iu © a s; his object of organizing preparations for his intended rising of the people against their þÿoppressors an object which, it is scarcely needed to say, required extreme caution and tact, as well as boldness, though he believed that the general sentiment of the people was already strongly disposed to a movement ior independence. With this view, he exerted himself, in many ways, to establish a personal popularity and personal relations, as extensively as possible, with the country people of all the surrounding region, the quajiros, every one of whom is more accustomed to the saddle than to any other seat, so that they may be called a population of cavalry, whom a very little 'rainiut;, under the inspiration of such a leader, would make a mounted force inferior to none in the world. He employed every mode in his power to make I himself personally familiar with them, to win , their confidence, and to attach them bv services and favours þÿ an operation in which, there. An intimate friendship xvith Espar- I always lavish and careless ol money, he spent with an unreserved hand. | Mingling thus familiarly among the qijajiros, in their own costume, and as rate of | I themselves, lie prepared them to tie in teadiness for the approaching day. Aided by (he doe to his rank, I fie brilliancy of his military reputation as i fie well-known bravest and boldest ulhcer of Cuba, his geneiosity and character for humanity and good-nature, he thus established an influence such as made him always confident that the whole region

would rise at fits voice whenever he should j summon the people to rally round the flag of liberty and independence. Having determined, early in 1848, that the proper lime had arrived, fie was onlv induced by some friends, to postpone his intended rising for a short lime, in order to await the itsull of some communications winch had proceeded from a highly distinguished American officer in Mexico, who knew the stale of public feeling in the island. This de.ay led, through an accidental cause, to the discoveiy ot Ins plan by the Government, and the sudden arrest ot Ins friends, and the necessity of his own precipitate embaikation tor this country, from whose friendly shores he hoped soon to he able to retuin. His plan for Cuba has always been independence and annexation to the American 1 Union. After Ins escape he was condemned to death. Among his papers, seized by the Government, was a letter to the Queen, resigning his commission, which was to have been sent to tin) Captain-General a day or two before the rising. This has been described, bv one who lias seen it, as a very noble and beautilul production, finely reconciling the duly of military honour with that of patriotism. Against the persons who had been arrested (some ol them, perhaps, with reason, and I some without,) no evidence existed, and the greater part were released, some being sent out of (he country. Lopez himself escaped in a vessel called the Neptune, and soon after landed at Rristol, R. 1. ITom that time down tu the attack

made on Cardenas, by an armed fotce, of which he was at the head, his name was always mentioned in connexion with the invasion of Cuba. On the 15th of May, 1830, three divisions consisting of (!09 men, of the Cuban expedition, off the Islands of Mugeres, near Yucaten, concentrated on board the steamer Creole. On the 19th of May,

Lopez, between two arid three þÿo clockin the morning, landeu at Cardenas, and losing between thirty and forty men, and killing many on the island, took the town. Subsequentiv, the invading force abandoned it, and. dost Iv pursued by the Spanish war steamer IY/.ariio, arrived at Key West, where ffle Creole was seized by the United States revenue oflicers. Oil the 27th of May, Lopez was arrested at Savannah, for his connexion with the Cuban expedition. No delay being granted by the district judge to procure evidence against him, he was discharged, amid the cheers of a iarge cfowd. On the 15. h of July, iorty-lwo of the Contoy prisoners (passengers) wcie liberated by the Spanish authorities, and were taken to þÿl ensacola by tiie United Stales ship Albany. Ten of them were retained for trial. On ihe 21st of July the Grand Jury of tiie United Stales District Court at New Oi leans found a line bill against Lopez and fifteen others, for violating the Act of 1818. The Government failed in making out its ease against one or two of the parties, and finally abandoned the prosecution. From that point the spirit of a new invasion seemed in gain an impetus, and a second expedition was prepared in the Summer o; the present year. With Lopez at its head, it started for Cuba from New Orleans, in the steamer þÿ1 ampero, and landed at Morrillo, Cuba, at eleven þÿo clock at night, on ihe Utfi of August. It seems to have consisted of about 480 men, many ol whom have ( aid the j penally of theii rashness, either by death or

imprisonment. Among these was Lopez himself. Worn down with fatigue, he was taken by Casteneda, an agent of the Spanish authorities, at Los l'iuos de Rangel, on the 29th of August, the whole of his forces having been dispersed, and himself resting, after wandering on foot, almost starved, and overcome only by nature herself. Colonel Fieron the Governor ofGuadeloupe quitted the Colony yesterday, embarking on board of the steamer Castor, bound to St. Thomas, intending fake to passage in the English steamer, to return to France. On leaving the island the Governor addressed the following Proclamation to the Inhabitants of Guadeloupe : Inhabitants of Guadeloupe ! The Minister of Marine, in a Despatch dated the 23rd September, 1851, announces to me the decree of the President of the Republic of the 15th of that the month, Navy, appointing Mr. Aubry to Bailleul, as my successor the Go- ot vernment of Guadeloupe and its dependencies. At the same time the Minister informs me, that in accordance with the suggestion furnished by me, the deemed necessary to replace it lias been government of Guadeloupe under the regulations prescribed in theOrdinanccs of 1827 and 1833. I arrived among you on the 11th October, 1848, and left you on the 17th May, 1849. You know my proceedings during that period, and you have been able to judge of my conduct. When the President of the Republic entrusted to me on the 9th November, 1849, the functions of Governor of Guadeloupe and its dependencies, with was assurance that its full confidence the given to me, I also received the special mission to pursue a conciliatory course amidst the people, towards the pacific arrangement of all causes of dissention, which could exist berween the different classes of the population ; furthermore

1 was directed þÿ Such must bethe point which you will incessantly keep in view, nevertheless remaining always prepared to check or punish in a prompt and energetic, manner t lie slightest attempt at disorder or abuse of the þÿlaws. Appreciating the extent of this duty, I could not fail to understand its importance; and it has been my sincere study. May I be permitted to believe that 1 have fulfilled the same, when I compare the present state of t he colony to what it was at the time of my arrival? At that time you will remember the court of justice was occupied with the legal proceedings against þÿ one hundred and twenty persons accused of being implicated in þÿ þÿLamentin of Sainte Rose þÿ the events of þÿ La þÿGabare, of Port Louis and Marie þÿGalantc, which occurred during my absence. The planters were trembling with alarm at the extent of the disorder. A g riculture was almost abandoned ; and the lately emancipated people were sub jeet to threats, and intimidation of for feiting their liberty, if they did not fl) from labour, until the time predicted oi announced to be at hand, for the indiscriminate division of lands. It was under these lamentable impressions that the elections for members of the Legislature took place in June, 1849,

anil had proved the cause or the pretext tor those sanguinary collisions which we have had reason to deplore. The Legislative Assembly have pronounced on this matter. I was called upon, and it was my duty to ordain a new election, in accordance with the respite determined by the electoral law of the 15th of March. Imperious necessity, having for its object the public security, I could not justify any delay in the accomplishment of these regulations. At the same time, it was my duty also to proceed with the þÿ municipal þÿelections, to replace the þÿ Mayors and þÿAldermen, the municipal counsellors of the ancient law, whose term of service was about to expire, and which had not been prorogued, although my predecessor had given notice to the Minister. I The most perfect order has been strictly observed during these proceedings, and the people have proved themselves worthy of the confidence T had placed in them. Every individual knew that he would enjoy full and entire liberty, and none could remain in ignorance þÿ that I possessed within myself the firmness and energy necessary to check or pre- vent every renewal of collisions. j If subsequently 1 have been compelled, owing to the incendiary tires in the town of Pointe-a-Pitre, to inflict on the colony þÿ a state of þÿsiege, this determination was with the object of prosecuting, arresting and bringing to a speedy trial, the criminals who by the ordinary course of justice, would believe I their being able to evade the penalty

due to their crime by the various forms and delays which would he observed. The military tribunal has been austere, energetic, and yet lenient ; its decisions show it ; but it has at the same time proved efficacious to 'check the growing evil, and prevent the extension which it threatened. I am happy in being able to affirm at this moment that for the last þÿ five þÿmonths no civil affair has been carried before the military tribunal, and that the ordinary courts of law are free from criminal prosecutions. Such is the state of tilings þÿ which presents itself all over the colony the þÿ and peace the products of this year most perfect order, labour prove that the industry of man has been i a seat at that Board. fully devoted to labour, the flattering expectations relative to the lorthcoming crop again confirm it, the amicable intercourse between the citizens is another source of gratification, the planters and labourers represent one family, there exists a reciprocal confidence, having for its iiasis fairness and equity ; ibis state of things inherent, is and ! believe myself authorised to say that it justifies my proceedings and the performance of mv duty equally as well as the case of Street, recently put complete Leonard Seneca! at Digue, lately decided, and is another evidence of the truth of my assertions. The second section of the Law of the 9th February 1829 defines the authority of the Governors as I have performed them until now, hut by a Ministerial decree of the 29th April 1851 these pow-

ers have been withdrawn from me, to be intrusted, fully and in an absolute manner to the Governor of Martinique, by giving to him the title of Governor General. Crushed, annihilated in my rank and dignity, by a decision contrary to that which is right, I caused immediately to he announced to the Minister of Marine, my formal refusal to accept the objectionable position which he wished to force on me. The following order has been issued by the police authorities of Rreslau : þÿ tual Repository, and a most important " It has several times happened during the performances at the theatre that a part of the public, particularly in the parterre, have given tokens of their displeasure when patriotic airs have been played, or when patriotic passages have been spoken on the stage, while allusions of a revolutionary description have been received by loud" applause. þÿ Such demonstrations of had political sentiments and all improper noises generally in the theatre cannot be tolerated. 1'lie police agents and gendarmes charged with the preservation of order in the theatre are strictly ordered to turn all those who offend in the above manner out of the house, and, according to circumstances, to arrest them. If the

disturbers of the peace are not to he recognized, the whole port of the house from which 1 he improper noise proceeds is to be cleared by the police, the clearance to he made, if necessary, by the military force. The visitors of the'theaearnestly requested, both in the public interest and tin ir own, to prevent themselves in future every demonstration of the above prohibited description. " Breslau, November 0." The order will cause more bad blood than the cause of it. A chance-collected body like a theatre audience cannot be made a solidarite for the good behaviour of all, according to the police estimate of decorum. Too much is also expected of the inferior police agents, who are only human, and from a wish to \ show their zeal have an exaggerated

They are the dissolvers of every kind of social gathering. They put aii end to halls, prayer meetings, and sermons, picnic parties, lectures on political economy, in which they have been known to mistake scientific terms for abuse of the constables, and now they are to clear the theatres it a political allusion is too much applauded or too much hissed. Suppose hot li demonstrations are made at onre, as generally happens. The whole audience must be confronted by a company of grenadiers descending by the footlights with fixed bayonets. It is remarkable that the theatre should he lieid more sarrcd than the Senatehouse. The galleries of the Chambers hiss and applaud the lion, deputies, according to their speeches, as long and loudly they like, hut no police order as has ever made that an "improper noise." In what temper is it expected an expelled theatre audience goes home? One of angelic satisfaction doubtless, and full of blessings, not loud, hut deep, of "the authorities." There is nothing like a very sensitive, very meddling, and police for sowing the seed of revolutions. Mr. Editor, Dear Sir, In your paper of the 1st instant, yon, in speaking ot the want of compensation, so severely felt by the Planters of this Island, observe: that "the weekly payments are in almost all eases advanced by the Royal Treasury." This ill-judged remark, I beg leave to contradict, as to the best of my knowledge, the Royal Treasury does not, at present, advance one cent to any Estate to meet weekly payments. As I do not think it necessary to support a good cause by incorrect statements, I avail myselfof this opportunity o correct the above remark. I am, Sir, yours, II. WE thank " II" for the information imparled in his communication. The " illjudged remark," as he observes, was made In/ " to support us, we say, not from any bad motive, nor a good cause by incorrect statements but having heard, for sometime past, that some of the planters were advanced certain sums from the State Treasury, to pay the labourers, we thought that this favor was yet extended to them. This, however, docs not mend the ease of the planters, it only shows that they arc exhausting their little means, ami that is previous little, to keep up the cultivation of their estates. þÿ Edt. 1 New York Herald. rather Ilalliow's Farewell Address. To the Citizens oe the United States. Dearey Beloved Friends : þÿ Mv mission amongst you closes to-day. I cannot take my linal departure from the shores of your great and prosperous country, without publickly recording mv deep and grateful appreciation of the

generous sympathy, the delicate attention, and the unremitting kindness which T have experienced in every section of this vast Union. The nohle reception which you have spontaneously tendered to a stranger, known merely as an humble missionary in the cause of moral reform, proves the devotion of your people to the interests of humanity, however feebly championed, and has endeared America and her people to me hv a thousand ties too sacred for utterance. Though t he renewed attacks of a painful and insidious malady, have rendered impossible that I could (without imminent danger to my life), make those public exertions which were never spared by me in the days of my health and ot my vigor, I yet thank heaven, have been instrumental in adding to the ranks of temperance over (500,000 disciples in America. I have been much cheered during the past week, by the receipt ol' letters from all parts of t lie States, hearing unimpeachable testimony to the strict fidelity with which the voluntary obligation is observed. I need scarcely add, that virtue, and the duties which icligion inculcates, together, with peace, plenty, domestic comfort, health, and happiness, have everywhere followed in its train. I cannot omit this opportunity of bearing my grateful testimony to the generous and valuable co-operation w hich I have received, in the prosecution of my mission, from the public press of America. Whatever may be the party or sectional differences that separate

s "j?» © Jfe © a Air $ it a, those influential expositors of public opinion, all recognized, in the simple principle which I enunciated, a common ground of paternal union ; and acting in the Christian spirit have, with scarcely an exception, ever freely tendered their valuable support and advocacy to the cause of temperance, emphatically the cause of virtue, patriotism and morality. If the affectionate sympathy and kindness of the American people have at all times been generously extended to me during my tour, how much more intense has this noble feeling become as the period approached lor my departure? How can I find language to thank the generous, the high-souled, the noble Henry Clay, my disinterested advocate þÿ my dearly cherished friend ? IIovv can I express the measure of my obligation to the benevolent Wm. Corceran, of Washington ? to the public spirited and philanthropic Henry Grinnell ? to your merchant princes, E. K. Collins and Robert Kennitt? to the amiable and gifted archbishop of New York, whose delicate and unremitting attention will never be forgotten by his honored guest? to the host of kind friends in this city, in Philadelphia, Boston, Albany, New Orleans, St. Louis, Cincinnati, and through the Union, who have responded to Mr. Clay's appeal, and in their U.ire well present have furmslicd a memorial of gratitude and generosity too highly appreciated hv the object >f their sympathy and solicitude þÿ too deeply engraven on his heart to be ackiiov.!' I god in the hacknied phrases sanctioned by conventional usage. There

arc » motions of gratitude too intense for language to convey: were it otherwise, gladly would 1 attempt to give expression to my profound thanks to my gifted and amiable countrywoman, Jliss Catherine llays. Never will I forget the sympathy felt by that noble minded lady, or the spontaneous generosity (so characteristic of her Irish heart) which prompted her recent grateful and substantial compliment. Never will this noble act be forgotten by Father Mathew, and when his earthly pilgrimage is over, when his stewardship ceases, and he is called to a state of future existence, where even the envenomed shaft of the slanderer cannot reach, long may her honored name he pronounced with gratitude and respect by the sons and daughters of that beauteous isle which she loves so well. To my own beloved countrymen i most affectionately tender a few words of parting advice. You have, my dearly beloved friends, relinquished the land of your birth, endeared to you by a thousand fond reminiscences, to seek on these distant shores that remuneration for industry and toil too often denied you at home. You are presented here with a boundless Held of profitable employment, and every inducement held out to persevering industry. You arc received and welcomed into the great American family with feelings of sympathy, kindness and friendship. After a few years you become citizens of this great republic, whose vast territorial extent abounds in all the materials of mineral ngiictil-

ture and commercial wealth ; the avenues to honor and fame are liberally thrown open to you and to your children, and no impediment (save of your ow-n creation) exists to prevent you attaining the highest social and civic distinction, and will you any longer permit those glorious opportunities to pass unimproved, or, rather, will you not, by studying self respect, and acquiring habits suited to your new position, aspire to reflect honor alike on the land of your birth and of your adoption? I implore you, us I would with my dying breath, to discard forever those foolish þÿdivisions those insensate þÿquarrels those factious broils (too often, alas, the iruits of intemperance) in which yout count . i disgraced, the peace and order (if sock :y violated, and the laws of heaven trai; pled on and outraged. Oil, how painful i< the contrast between the feelings which generate those foolish local animosities amongst the common inhabitants of a country, the entire area of which would but form an inconsiderable section of some of the larger States ot this I nion, and that broad and comprehensive spirit of patriotism which makes every inhabitant of this mighty republic þÿ from the Atlantic to the Pacific þÿ from Maine to California þÿ <5 glory in m the title of an American citizen. Friends and fellow-countrymen þÿ I now bid yon reluctant, a final farewell. A a few hours more will separate me from the hospitable shores of America, foi ever. 1 carry with me, to " the pooi old country," feelings of respect and at

tachment for its people, thnt neither time nor distance can obliterate. Citizens of the I nitcd States þÿ I fervently pray that the Almighty Disposer of human events, in whose hands are the destinies of nations, may continue those blessings and favors which vou have so long O enjoyed þÿ that your progress in every private and public virtue may keep pace with your unexampled prosperity þÿ that, you and your children's children may he ever true to the great destiny that awaits you, and to the spirit, of those institu tions und. r the fostering care of which you have so rapidly progressed. May your country still extend the hand ot succor to lie helpless exile, afford an asylum to the persecuted, and a home to the oppressed þÿ and thus inseparably connect her future destiny with the interests of universal humanity. Citizens of the ( nited States, and be loved countrymen þÿ again adieu ! May heaven pour its choicest blessings or. your favored land, is the farewell prayer of Your devoted and affectionate friend, Theobald Mathew.

St. Thomas Times, December 2, 1851. We were informed this morning by a gentleman that a letter bad been received here by the steamer from Windward yesterday, which gave the details ot the Fire, reported by a private arrival to have broken out at Basseterre, Guadeloupe, and which was stated to lie one of a most calamitous kind. The public has accordingly felt anxious to he made acquainted with tlie particulars of a conflagration that had been made to appear of so grave a character: and we, in our desire to serve tlm public,- sought the information fJom the quarter which we were directed to. We arc therefore happy in being able to contradict, the greatly exaggerated report, of Monday about the lire, and to state that instead of the same having lasted for three (lays, and destroying almost the whole of Basseterre, its duration was only of three hours, burning down two houses, and consuming property to the probable ev tent ol six thousand dollars. The seamen and marines of a frigate lying in pot t. are said to have done adinirabls well in suppressing the lire.
Ii will he seen by our extracts from flic St. Luna Palladium, that a report had been current in that colony of the

CZ Cholera having reached Guadeloupe, and the Yellow Fever-broke out in the Island of Martinique J'his is certainly nothing more than rumour, hut yet sonic apprehension should he felt lest the same prove true, and it is with a view to guard against the introduction into this Island of any loathsome disease that we have felt it our duty to direct the attention of the authorities to the subject, þÿ in order to be made acquainted whether there be any foundation for the report, and if so to afford ample time for enforcing the Quarantine Regulations against vessels arriving here from those places. þÿ " Prevention is better than cure." - EE»

St. Thomas Times, D, amber 13. 1851 Oi'tt readers may very well remember that about eighteen months ago our columns were occupied with a series of letters treating on the sacredness of the Sabbath-day. Those letters we arc sensible received the earnest attention ol that class of the community who are hv birth and education belonging to those countries where violating the Sabbath is viewed as a sacrilege of the highest degree. Custom, however, in this Island, we are sorry to say, had brought it to be considered a very venial offence against þÿreligion particularly as it had for firmly years been practised by those who possess a powerful influence in the country. Under such circumstances it may easily he supposed that the letters we refer to þÿ discountenanced as they were hv thoi-e from whom better things might have been ex þÿnected failed to produce the de sired effect. But time, and tide, and train bring with them their changes, and with others, a change ot feeling among the Clerks of St. Thomas has arisen in relation to the evils connected with the principle of being ex pec ted tube wrought as hard on the Sunday as on any other day of the week; and having become impressed with the injustice and sinfulness ot the rule, they have unitedly proceeded to lav their case, by memorial, before His Excellency Governor Redder. sen, praying that the inviolnhlcness of the Christian Sabbath niav in this Island he henceforth maintained by law, in order that they may he relieved from so unreasonable an exaction. It is very

pleasing to know that the memorial in question is supported hv many of our most respectable and influential Merchants, who have attested to the fact by certifying to the same at the bottom of the memorial of their own dependents. We possess every confidence for the success of the memorial, not only on account of hearing on its face the stamp of religion, justice and law, but also because of the man who is called upon to deal with it. It is indeed a pitiful case to behold in a community men of christian educations, and an enlarged and extensive knowledge of the world, presuming to select for themselves, three, four, or live of the ten commandments of (ion, and to jecting the others as inconvenient in connection with their worldly affairs. Any man possessing a sound moral convictioi ol the necessity ol living up to sotnt ofthe commandments, ought, if he would i t : son rightly, see that the whole should he

observed in like manner ; because, it one ela ; of men are allowed to violate the Jouith commandment without penalty, why should another class he punished for violating the eighth. And we are sure that no merchant in this Island would like to entertain the idea that a man could go into his (the merchant's) store and break the 8th commandment, without the certainty of punishment þÿ then why should he expect to lie exempt Iroui obeying the fourth, for both are God's especial decree, and to Him, if disregarded, equal misdemeanours.

Mn. Editor, The period has arrived when the inhabitants oftliis Island are again called upon to elect a new Burgher Council. It is the opinion of many persons that triennial elections would lie preferable to the present short term of one year, þÿ a period which must be considered too short to adiuil of any ones acquiring the necessary experience to become useful or efficient, þÿ as (he members may scarcc- Iv be said to have entered upon the duties of their office before their functions are to cease, unless re-elected. What Napoffon hid for Fp.ancf, and for himself. þÿ lie left freedom chained, equality compromised by posthumous institutions, feudalism parodied, without power to exist, human conscience resold, philosophy prescribed, prejudices encouraged, the human mind diminished, instruction materialised and concentrated in the pure sciences alone, schools converted into barracks, literature degraded by censorship, or bumbled baseness, national representation perverted, election abolished, the arts enslaved, commerce destroyed, credit annihilated, navigation suppr Cfi s ed, international hatred revived, the people oppressed, or enrolled in the armv, paying in blood or taxes the amj bition of an unequalled soldier, bntcovcring O with the O gn at name of France the contradictions of the age, the miseries and degradation of the country. This is the founder ! This is the man ! þÿ a man instead of a revolution ! þÿ a man instead of a country ! þÿ a man instead of a nation ! Nothing after him ! nothing around hint hut his shadow, making sterile the eighteenth century, absorbed and concentrated in himself alone. Personal glorv will be always spoken of as characterizing the age of Napoleon ; but it will never merit the praise bestowed upon that of Augustus, of Charlemagne, and of Louis XIV. There is no age ; there is only a name ; and this nnmcsignifies nothingto humanitv but himself. False in institutions, for he retrograded ; false in policy, for he debased ; false in morals, for he corrupted ; false in civili-

zation, for lie oppressed ; false in diplomacy, for he isolated þÿ he was only true in war; for lie shed torrents of human blood. But what can we then allow him ' His individual genius was great ; but it was the genius of materialism. þÿ His intelligence was vast and clear, but it was intelligence of calculation. He counted, he weighed, be measured ; but he felt not ; he loved not; he sympathised with none; lie was a statute rather than a man Therein lay his inferiority to Alexander andtoCsesar: lie resembled the Hannibal of the aristocracy. Few men haw thus been moulded, and moulded cold All was sold, nothing gushed fm-ih, hi that, mind nothing was moved. His nic tslic nature was felt even )P hi- stvle

He was, perhaps, the greatest writer of liuman events since Macliiaveh Much superior to (besar in the account of his campaigns, his style is not t lie written expression alone, it is the action. Every sentence in his pages is, so to speak, the counter-part and counter-impression of the lact. There is neither a letter, a sound, or a colour wasted between the lact and tiie word, and the word is himself. His phrases concise, hut struck oil with ornament, rceal those times when Bnjazct and Charlemnnge not knowing how to write their names at the bottom of their imperial acts, dipped their hands in ink or blood, and applied them with all their articulations impressed upon the parchment. It was not the signature; it was the hand itself ol the hero thus lixed eternally before the eves ; and such were the pages ol his campaigns dictated by Napoleon þÿ the very soul of movement, of action, and of combat. His Portrait in 1814. þÿ The empire had made him old before his time. Gratified ambition, satiated pride, the delights of a palace, a luxurious table, a voluptuous couch, youthful wives, complaisant mistresses, long vigils, sleepless nights, divided between labour and festive pleasures, t he habit ofconstant riding which made him corpulent, þÿ all tended to deaden his limbs and enervate his faculties. An early obesity overloaded with flesh. His cheeks, formally streaked with muscles and hallowed by the working of genius, were broad, full and overhanging, like those of Otho, in the

Roman models of the empire. An excess of bile mingling with the blood, gave a yellow tint to the skin, which at a distance looked like a varnish of pale gold on his countenance. His lips still preserved their Grecian outline and steady grace, passing easily from a smile to a menace. Ilis solid bony chin formed an appropriate iias«- for his features. His nose was hut a line, thin and transparent. The paleness of his cheeks gave greater brilliancy to the blue of his eyes. His forehead seemed to have widened from the scantine ss of liis thin black hair, which was falling from the moisture of continual thought, ft might he said that his head, naturally small, had increased to a size to give ample scope between his temples for the machinery and combinations of a mind, every thought of which was an empire. The map of tlic world seemed to have In i 11 em rusted on that reflective head. Rut it was beginning to yield: and he inclined it on his breast while crossing his arms like Frederick þÿII. an attitude and gesture which lie appeared to affect. Unable any longer to seduce his courtiers and his soldiers by the charm of youth, it was evident he wished to fascinate tlicm by the rough, pensive, and disdainful character of himself þÿ of his model in his latter days. He moulded himself, as it were, into the statute of reflection before his troops, who gave him the nickname of Vathrr Thoughtful. He assumed the pone of destiny. Something rough, rude, and savage in his movemen's revealed his southern and insular

0 w @ <D A T origin. The man of the Mediterranean broke outconstnntly through the Frenchman. His nature too great and too powerful for the part he had to play, overflowed on all occasions. lie bore no reseniblar.ee to any of the men around him. Superior and altogether different, he was an offspring of the sun, of the sea, and of the battle þÿfield out of the element even in his own palace, and a stranger even in his own empire. Such was at this period the profile, the bust, and physiognomy of Napoleon. Observation. þÿ A dervise was journeying alone in the desert, when two merchants suddenly met him ; "Yon have " Indeed lost a camel," said he, to the merchants. we have," they replied. " Was lie not blind in his right eye, and lame in his let t leg?" said the dervise. "He I was," replied the merchants. " Had he not lost a front tooth ?" said the dervisc. ' He had," rejoined ihe merchants. "And was he not loaded with honey on one side, and wheat on the other?" " Most certainly he was," they replied ; "and as you have seen him so lutclv, and marked him so particularly, von can. in all probability, conduct us unto him." "My friends," said the dervise, I have never seen your camel, nor ever heard of him, hut from you." "A pretlv story, truly," said the merchants : ' hut where are the jewels which formed a part of his cargo?" "1 have neither seen your camel, nor your jewels," repeated the dervise. On this they seized his person, and forthwith hurried him before the cadi, where, on the strictest

search, nothing could be found upon him, nor could any evidence whatever tie adduced to convict him, cither of falsehood, or of theft. Tlicy were then about to proceed against him <u a sorcerer, when the dervise, with great calmness, thus addressed the court: þÿ "I have been much amused with your surprise, and own that there has been some ground for your suspicions ; but I have lived long, and alone ; and I can lind ample for observation, even in a desert. I scope knew that I had crossed t he track of a camel that had strayed from its owner, because on the same route ; I "knew that the ani- I saw no mark of any human footstep mal was blind in one eye, because it had cropped the herbage only on one side of its path; and 1 perceived that it was lame in one leg, from the faint impression which that particular foot, had produced upon the sand ; I concluded that the animal had lost one tooth, because, wherever it had grazed, a small tuft of herbage had been left uninjured in the centre of its bite. As to that which formed the burthen of the beast, the busy ants informed me that it was corn on the one side, and the clustering flies that it was honey on the other. þÿ Colton. Enron.

8 Proclamation ok M. Aubry Baili.eul, to the Inhabitants of Guadeloupe. " Inhabitants of Guadeloupe! "Called upon by the confidence of the President of the Republic to the honor to direct the administration of this colony, I arrive among you. impressed with the wise and considerate views, the accomplishment of which has been dcligated to me by the Chief of the State, and determined to consecrate to you all my devotion, and all my efforts. " The moment has arrived to restore to the exercise of the functions of Governor of Guadeloupe the full conditions established by the organization of 1827. "Fortunate in bringing to you this pledge of the the vernment of good intentions of the Go- Mother Country, 1 demand of you, in return, to facilitate 1 he success of my mission, by a frank union to the þÿauthority guardian of the rights of all, and the impartial protection of every interest and by extending to me þÿ your confidence which I believe myselt deserving of. "To repeat to you that 1 come here With the firm intention to guarantee the principle of equality among the citizens would cause it to be supposed that there would be found among you some persons who require sucli assurance. " Planters, artizans, mechanics, merchants, proprietors, do not be mistrustful. Let there lie perfect faith in the system of pledges irrevocably established in the Colonies. Turn your attention with the greatest ardour to your labours or occupation, and soon all, without any distinction, will acknowledge that you have in

reality but one enemy þÿ the spirit of division and disorder! this is the veritable cause of the allliction or evil to which this colony has been for some time exposed. " Turn aside and abandon those who by fallacious promises, by a system of excitement or perfidious insinuations, seek to keep up this division ; banish from your minds all sentiments hatred, of confide in the impartiality of justice, within whose sanctuary there could never be any preferences for any class of citizens, "and you will soon see revived, with order, harmony and labor, the ancient prosperity of your beautiful colony, so long known asthe I'atriolic Guadeloupe. " i am happily informed that this vear's crop, prepared and gathered by free labour, has been more advantageous than the preceding, notwithstanding the atmospherical circumstances, which have counteracted vour last labours ; and that the planters' aspects at this moment offer the hope ot greater advantages for the coming year. " Respecting the laws on Sugars and on Ranks, which are already in operation in the colonics, will soon be added those which will regulate the administrative, legislative, and financial departments ; therefore, as early as the approaching year you will enjoy, by the - election of a general council, the manage ment of your colonial interests. The ameliorations will not be limited to this, vou will soon have the proofs. "Inhabitants of Guadeloupe ! þÿ I do not wish to dissemble my impression, even on a serious subject. I do not see,

in the continuation of this exceptional system to which the colony yet remains subject, but one of the means necessary to conclude the work of pacification, and to cement order, without which there could be no real liberty. I nder my administration, like under that of my honored predecessor, the state ofsiege, as long as it will be maintained by the national Legislative Assembly, will not be enforeed with unnecessary severity. « Protection and security for the inhabitants industrious and submissive to the laws.

My constant efforts will be devoted to that purpose, but to obtain it effectually, it is necessary that the good citizens show a cordial and spontaneous union to the authorities. "ISo one among you will witness the termination of your differences, and of the exceptional system thereby rendered necessary, with a greater satisfaction than I would feel on such an occasion. "Inhabitants of Guadeloupe! þÿ You love and respect the religion of your fathers, and you will have appreciated the fostering care of the Government of the metropolis, who recently sent among you a worthy and pious Bishop, to direct the Clergv in the lslar.d, and to inspire them with his examples. " Your children will receive the great boon of elementary arid religious instruczeal and attention by the ' Brother tion, which is imparted to them with Ploermel' and by the ' Sisters of Saint Joseph.' "You will always see me active in giving my support to such laudable efforts; and soon, with the aid of Divine Providence, the sentiments of christian charity will be developed your in breasts, so that it will prove that fraternity can never be a vain word." Keutsch, in behalf of the Committee appointed to gather Subscriptions, stated that as they had now 80 Subscribers, they were of opinion that a commencement could be made ; and as the functions of the Committee, in whose behalf he spoke, were now at an end, he proposed that another Committee should be appointed to frame the Constitution and Laws of the Institution. A letter from Government was then read, stating, that at the suggestion of Ilis Excellency the Governor and the representation of the Minister of Finances, His Majesty had most graciously sanctioned various immunities for the promotion of this Institution. The following is the most particular : that hooks of deposits in this or tl lose Savings Banks which in time future, may be established in St. Croix, may be expedited on unstamped paper, and that such deposits shall not be liable to seizure or sequestration for debts. We have the unpleasant duty this afternoon to chronicle the loss of the American barque Mary Irvine, of Philadelphia, J. Taylor, Master. This vessel was hound to lioston U. S., from Antwerp, deeply laden with dry-goods, hardware, A:c., and after having been driven off the coast of America, was making for this port, when on Sunday noon last she struck on the Anegada reef, in about 5 fathoms water, and soon after became a total wreck. The weather has been so rough as to prevent the possibility of div ers recovering as yet any portion of her cargo. One man met with a watery grave by the upsetting of Ins boat while endeavouring to rescue the crew of the unfortunate vessel. The 2nd mate and men of the barque arrived here yesterday from Tortola, and are now umter the protection of the American Consul, awaiting the arrival of the commander and chief mate, who remained by the wreck. It has often been matter of surprise to us that a suitable Lighthouse has not long ere this been erected at Anegada, for the safety and guidance of vessels of all nations traversing t he waters in the vicinity of that dangerous place. It would occupy too much space to enumerate the different noble ships that have been wrecked, and the valuable cargoes lost among the British Virgin Islands within our recollection. Suffice ittosay that we see ample cause why the attention of tiie Government of the greatest commercial nations, viz England, France and America, should be directed to the subject, in order that by their combined
endeavours some means may speedily he devised, by the erection of a stationary or floating Beacon, for the protection of the lives and property of their subjects and citizens. þÿ Ibid.

Bumiii.l, left the Island of Barbados, in ballasttrim, on her voyage to Newr-llaven, and was cast away on the shoals of Anegada, on the morning of the 21st instant, about a mile from the spot where the Mary Irvine was stranded. colonial trader and passage boat. Wesincerely hope the owners of the vessel will employ her, even, if only for a very limited period, in running between tlrese Islands, as we feel convinced they would meet with success, in their new enterþÿprise on which every Colony would cheerfully encourage. A steamer capable of affording comfortable accommodation to passengers, and of carrying a considerable freight, running from Barbados to St. Thomas, calling at the intermediate ports, would no doubt yield the ow ners a handsome return on tin capital invested. PUJ5LICAriON. ll.ws Dii'.mar Fkederik Feddersei, hiiifr/it of Danvcbrog, tiovernor of tlio Danish NVestindia Possessions, Make known: That His Majesty the King, on the report of the Minister of Finances to this effect, iias been most graciously pleased under date of the lGtli of September last to empower the Government to put in force the following rules as regulations for the pilots of St. Croix, and, for the future, to make such alterations in the direction of the same of a merely regulative nature, as from time to time may he deemed necessary and proper. Regulations for the pilots of St. Croix: The , pilots and the crew of the pilot Iboat shall dwell 011 Protestant Quay, which tliey must not leave without the permission of the headpilot, giving notice at the same time where they may lie found, in case their services should be required. They ought not, without necessity, to be granted permission to be absent during the night, and shall always be on duty at daybreak, under a fine not exceeding £">. 2. The sailors, belonging to the pilotboat, sluill by turns be on the look out

for vessels standing for t lie harbour and either of the pilots shall constantly he on guard on the Quay and frequently inspect the man on with the the look out. for As a soon as a vessel, signal pilot hoisted, heaves in sight,, or a signal is made front the Point battery, that a vessel is in sight, it is immediately to he reported to the pilot on duty, and it devolves then on the head pilot, if lie be present, to give the necessary order with regard to which of the pilots shall go to sea and whether a sailing boat or a rowboat shall be used. 3- . . The sailor on guard shall during his watch stay in a place, from which he has the best look out, ami whenever the pilot on duty leaves in order to meet the vessel, standing for the harbour, the other pilot shall take his guard at once, if he be present, or if not, as soon as he returns. Both pilots are never to be allowed tube absent from the Quay at the same time, except on duty. $ 1. Win 'never it is doubtful, in consequence of haziness or from other causes, whether the vessel in sight has hoisted a signal for a pilot, it is nevertheless the duty of the pilot to go out to meet her. If a vessel has hoisted a signal of distress, the pilot on duty shall report it without delay to the Inspector of Customs, in order that the necessary arrangements mav be made. 5. Whenever a pilot has brought a vessel into port, he must not leave her until she is come to anchor and is well secured ; and whenever he pilots a vessel out of port he must not leave her until he

has brought her so far out as he is in duty hound. No other persons hot the pilots are 6V allowed to pilot any vessel or to go on hoard any coming vessel, which has made signal for a pilot ; but this does not prohibit fishermen or other individuals well acquainted with the coast to go on board for the purpose of cautioning against any dangerous shoal or shallow the vessel may have approached, whilst the pilot boat is not yet ori its way out, <ir when the vessel has hoisted a signal of distress. The | ilotboats are, in order to distinguish them always to he tarnished with a broad streak of red canvas in the middle of the white mainsail, and the row boats to carry a red Hag, hoisted on an upright stall'. ' The place where vessels are to anchor in the harbour, is to be pointed out by the pilots, and it is in particular incumbent on the head pilot to exercise the necessary superintendence in this respect. W hcncver he deems it necessary that a vessel changes her anchorage, the master is hound to warp his vessel, under the guidance of the head pilot, to ihc place pointed out by him, for which, however, the pilot shall not receive any lee or payment. The pilots are to act in strict conformity with the harbour regulations and it is in particular the duty of the headpilot to see tliem complied with. a. If a vessel in clear weather stands for the harbour, making signal for a pilot, and receives damage, evidently owing to any remissness on the part oi the pilot or to his not coining on board in proper

time, the pilot or pilots, who have neglected their duty, are to pay damages, and even if the vessel has sustained no injury, they are to he liable to a fine, a rest or dismissal, according to the circumstances of t he case. % 9. A pilot, who from ignorance, remissness or error runs a vessel on shore or

& <0 i ? It 8, pilots her in shall tains injury, such a manner that she sus- repair the damage and will he prosecuted and punished according to the nature of the offence. Whenever a pilot coming on board for the purpose of piloting a vessel, should he found to he intoxicated or, during the time he remains on board as pilot, gets drunk, he will he punished the lirst time by the Inspector of Customs with a line, but the second time with dismissal, the case having previously been laid before the Government for its decision. $ 10. It is incumbent on the head pilot not only to perform the duties of a pilot, but also to attend to, that the harbour regulations are strictly complied with, that the buoys, warps, mooring anchors and the rest intended for the use and security of the shipping in the harbour are at all times kept in proper order. As soon as lie becomes aware of any defect in or of any injury done to said objects or to the pilotboat or any other part of the inventory, he shall report it, without delay to the Inspector of Customs, who lias the superintendence of ail matters connected with the harbour and pilotage. $ 11. At the end of every year the head pilot shall deliver to the Inspector of Customs a list of all the appurtenances of the harbour, intended for the security of the shipping, together with the necessary information in reference to the condition they are in, as also a list of the rest of the inventory with similar elucidations. $ 12. Every transgression of these rules,

PUBLICATION. h.w's pltmar Furderik Fr.ddf.nskm, Knight of Doantbrog, Governor u! :;;e Danish Westinilia Possessions, m \ k r knows : That His Majesty the King, on the report of the Minister of Finances to tips effect, lias been most e-racio: ! v pleased under date of the l(ith of September inst. to empower the Government to put in force the following : l les as regulations for the i: lots of St. Croix, and, for the future, to make such alterations in the direction of the same of a merely regulative nature, as from time to time may be d e; ted necessary and proper. Herniations tor the pilots of St. Croix: F The pilot and the crew of the pilotboat shall dwell on Protestant Quay, which they must not leave without the permission of the head pilot, giving notice at the same time where they may he found, in case their services should he required. The ought not, without necessity, to he granted permission to be absent during the night, and shall always |>e on duty at daybreak, under a line not exceeding $3. $ Z- The sailors, belonging to the pilotboat, shall by turns he on the look out for vessels standing for the harbour and either of the pilots shall constantly he on guard on the Quay and frequently inspect the man on ihe look out. As soon as a vessel, with the signal for a pilot hoisted, heaves in sight, or a signal is made from the Point battery, that a vessel is in sight, it is immediately to he reported to the pilot on duty, and it devolves then on the head pilot", if he' lie present, to give the necessary order with

regard to which of the pilots shall go to srni and whether a sailing boat or a rowboat shall be used. % :i. The sailor on guard shall during his watch stay in a place, from which he lias the best look out, and whenever the pilot on duty leaves in order to meet the vessel, standing for the harbour, the other pilot shall take his guard at once, if lie be present, or if not, as soon as he returns. Roth pilots are never to lie allowed to he absent from the (liiay at the same, time, except on dutv. A 4 Whenever it is doubtful, in consequence of haziness or from other causes, whether the vessel in sight has hoisted a signal for a pilot, ii is nevertheless the duty of the pilot to go out to meet her. if a vessel has hoisted a signal of dis-

KIKNIIAGC.X I»EIV $«ie tress, the pilot on duty shall report it without delay to the Inspector of Customs, in order that the necessary arrangements may be made. % 5. Whenever a pilot has brought a vessel into port, he must not leave her until she is come to anchor and is well secured ; and whenever he pilots a vessel out of port he must not leave her until lie has brought her so far out as he is in duty bound. $ (5- No other persons but the pilots are allowed to pilot any vessel or to go on hoard any coming vessel, which lias made signal for a pilot; hut this does not prohibit fishermen or other individuals well acquainted with the coast to go on board for the purpose of cautioning against any dangerous shoal or shallow the vessel may have approached, whilst the pilot boat is not yet on its way out, or when the vessel has hoisted a signal of distress. The pilotboats are, in order to distinguish them always to he furnished with a broad streak of red canvas in the middle of the white mainsail, and the row boats to carry a red flag, hoisted on an upright staff. $ 7. The place where vessels are to anchor in the harbour, is to be pointed out by the pilots, and it is in particular incumbent on the head pilot to exercise the necessary superintendence in this respect. Whenever he deems it necessary that a vessel changes her anchorage, the master is hound to warp his vessel, under the guidance of the head pilot, to the place pointed out by him, for which, however, the pilot shall not receive any

fee or payment. The pilots are to act in strict conformity with the harbour regulations and it is in particular the duty of the headpilot to see them complied with. H. If a vessel in clear weather stands for the harbour, making signal for a pilot, and receives damage, evidently owing to any remissness on the part of the pilot or to bis not coming on board in proper time, t fie pilot or pilots, who liaVe neglected their duty, are to pay damages, and even if the vessel has sustained no injury, they are to be liable to a fine, arrest or dismissal, according to the circumstances of tlie case. y. A pilot, who from ignorance, remissness or error runs a vessel on shore or pilots her in such a manner that she sustains injury, shall repair the damage and will be prosecuted and punished according to the nature of the offence. Whenever a pilot coming on board for the purpose of piloting a vessel, should be found to he intoxicated or, during the time he remains on hoard as pilot, gets drunk, lie will he punished the iirst time by the Inspector of Customs with a line, but the second time with dismissal, the case having previously been laid before the Government for its decision. $ 10. It is incumbent on the head pilot not only to perform the duties oi a pilot, hut

JWIAII I.V». also to attend to, that the harbour regulations are strictly complied with, that the buoys, warps, mooring anchors and ihc rest intended for the use and security ol ihe shipping in t lie harbour are at all times kept in proper order. As soon as lie becomes aware of any defect in or of any in jury done to said objects or to the pilotboat or any other part of the inventory, he shall report it, without delay to the Inspector of Customs, who has the Superintendence of all matters connected with the harbour and pilotage. 11. At the end ol every year the head pilot shall deliver to the Inspector of Customs a list of all the appurtenances of the harbour, intended for the security of the shipping, together with the necessary information in reference to the condition they are in, as also a list of the rest, of the inventory with similar elucidations. $ 12. Every transgression of these rules, remissness oi' the pilots in the performance of their duties, refractory conduct or disobedience of orders will he punished, unless otherwise directed by the above, either with a fine imposed by the Inspector of Customs or by the Government ; or, according to circumstances, with dismissal from service. In case of a transgression of a serious nature, it. will depend upon the decision of the Government, whether the offender is instantly to be dismissed or to he arraigned. If the offence in question has caused the loss of any revenue, the fine imposed ought at least to equal the amount

of the pilotage, which thus lias been lost, and in case of dismissal the offender ought likewise to lie compelled to make good the revenue thus lost. Which regulations, in conformity with the above Royal Resolution, is hereby put in force. Government of the Danish West-India Islands, St. Croix 23 rd December J851. EEDDEllSEN.

Mr. Editor, Sir ! In the St. Thomas Times of 3d Jan: I perused an editorial article, containing the following remarks; on which I beg leave to express an opinion. The Editor remarks : "That Rescripts, Proclamations, Ordinances or Rules, intended for the Government of an Island should be given to its population in a language understood only by its officials and public employ es, is a circumstance that we believe can no longer fail to arrest the serious attention of the public?" That a Danish Government should be expected to issue Rescripts &c., in a foreign language is in my opinion unreasonable, for in such a case they would certainly be held responsible for abundantly supplied with rain often is the case, not convey the exact the translation: which may, as very shade of meaning which the original Danish conveys. I think it therefore quite correct that Translations should be executed by the Editor or some other person, who of course, in cases where t lie translation is not rendered in exact agreement with the original, will be excused by the public; whereas if these translations were given by Government they would be held equally authoritative as the Original Danish. The population of St. Thomas is composed of persons speaking many languages, and if a portion who speak the English language have a right to demand of the Government, that their official documents he given them in that language, then in my opinion, the other portions have an equal right to make

similar demands. Such demands if granted, would give us an excellent specimen of a Polyglot Journal, and wold call for the establishment of an office of authorized translators þÿ an establishment which would hut add one more to the too many already » existing. a O

I would have it however to he understood, that 1 do not object to the necessity of having these publications translated, 1 wish merely to state that such a thing can not reasonably he expected from the Government, and consequently the duty is then left to the Editors o'f papers, who can either publish these translations in their columns (which by rendering their papers more useful would enlarge their subscription lists,) or separately in sheet form, which would also be of pecuniary benefit. I remain, Sir, Yours, truly, A.

Therefore, from the origin, the French statesmen have shown a due regard to the linanrial feature of this important question. Where they alledged ' political remembered palliate their acts, they expediency to the protection belonging to their loyal subjects, although in distant colonies. They understood that commerce must riot he annihilated ; that the þÿplanters men whose industry is deeply connected with

trade, men who amidst the most trying circumstances contributed largely to the advancement of the country, demanded, and were entitled to protection ; and the claims of trit fairs arid orphans could not be set aside. Under these circumstances, the principle of indemnity conld not he evaded; to have acted otherwise would have caused a general bankruptcy and ruin; the best interests of the colonies remained involved in the great experiment, and what was the result? The intelligence from the Islands continue to announce the favorable aspect of things; a powerful impulse is seen in every branch ol industry, and the statement which we publish today in regard to the conclusive exported presents quantity of sugar evidence that in the prompt payment ot the amount of Indemnity due to the late owners will be found the basis ol that large share of prosperity and improvement which we anticipate for the tuture þÿ without that mite of justice those valuable colonies would have been ruined.

PUBLICATION. IIans Ditmar Frederik Feodersf.n, Knight of Dannebrog, Governor of (lie Danish Westindm Possessions, M are known : That Ilis Majesty the King, on the report of the Minister of Finances to this effect, has been most graciously pleased under date of the I6th of September last to empower the Government to put in force the following rules as regulations for the pilots of St. Oroix, and, tor the future, to make such alterations in the direction of the same of a merely regulative nature, as from time to time may he deemed necessary and proper. Regulations tor the pilots ofSt. Croix: 1. The pilots and the crew of the pilotboat. shall dwell on Protestant Quay, which they must not leave without the permission of the headpilot, giving notice at the same time where they may he found, in case their services should he required. They ought not, without necessity, to he granted permission to he absent during the night, and shall always he on duty at daybreak, under a fine not exceeding 5. $ 2. The sailors, belonging to the pilotboat, shall by turns be on the look out for vessels standing for the harbour and either of the pilots shall constantly he on guard on the Quay and frequently inspect the man on the look out. As soon as a vessel, with the signal for a pilot hoisted, heaves in sight, or a signal is made from the Point battery, that a vessel is in sight, it is immediately to be reported to the pilot on duty, and it devolves then on the head pilot, if he be present, to give the necessary order with

regard to which of the pilots shall go to sea and whether a sailing boat or a rowboat shall be used. 3> The sailor on guard shall during his watch stay in a place, from which he has the best look out, and whenever the pilot on duty leaves in order to meet the vessel, standing for the harbour, the other pilot shall take his guard at once, if he be present, or if not, as soon as he returns. Roth pilots are never to be allowed to be absent from the Quay at the same time, except on duty. 4- Whenever it is doubtful, in consequence of haziness or from other causes, whether the vessel in sight has hoisted a signal for a pilot, it is nevertheless the duty of the pilot to go out to meet her. If a vessel has hoisted a signal of distress, the pilot on duty shall report it without delay to the inspector of Customs, in order that the necessary arrangements may be made. . 5. Whenever a pilot has brought a vessel into port, he must not leave her until

H\MIV<-i;\ I»I:\ iatc JAMJAR she is come to anchor and is well secured ; and whenever he pilots a vessel out of port he must not leave her until he has brought her so far out as he is in duty bound. G. No other persons but the pilots are allowed to pilot any vessel or to go on hoard any coming vessel, which has made signal for a pilot; but this does not prohibit fishermen or other individuals well acquainted with the coast to go on board tor the purpose of cautioning against any dangerous shoal or shallow the vessel may have approached, whilst the pilot boat is not yet on its way out, or when the vessel has hoisted a signal of distress. The pilotboats are, in order to distinguish them always to he furnished with a broad streak of red canvas in the middle of the white mainsail, and the row boats to carry a red tlag, hoisted on an upright staff. % 7. The place where vessels are to anchor in the harbour, is to be pointed out by the pilots, and it is in particular incumbent on the head pilot to exercise the necessary superintendence in this respect. Whenever he deems it necessary that a vessel changes her anchorage, the master is bound to warp his vessel, under the guidance of the head pilot, to the place pointed out by him, for which, however, the pilot shall not receive any fee or payment. The pilots are to act in strict conformity with the harbour regulations and it is in particular the duty of the headpilot to see them complied with. $ 8. If a vessel in clear weather stands for the harbour, making signal for a pilot,

and receives damage, evidently owing to any remissness on the part oi the pilot or to his not coming on board in proper time, the pilot or pilots, who have neglected their duty, are to pay damages, and even if the vessel has sustained no injury, they are to be liable to a fine, arrest or dismissal, according to the circumstances of the case. 9. A pilot, who from ignorance, remissness or error runs a vessel on shore or pilots her in such a manner that she sustains injury, shall repair the damage and will be prosecuted and punished according to the nature of the offence. Whenever a pilot coming on board for the purpose of piloting a vessel, should be found to be intoxicated or, during the time he remains on board as pilot, gets drunk, he will he punished the first time by the Inspector of Customs with a line, but the second time with dismissal, the case having previously been laid before the Government for its decision. $ 10. It is incumbent on the head pilot not only to perform the duties harbour also to attend to, that the of a pilot, but regulations are strictly complied with, that the buoys, warps, mooring anchors and the rest intended for the use and security of the shipping in the harbour are at all times kept in proper order.

issu. As soon as he becomes aware of any defect in or of any injury done to said objects or to the pilotboat or any other part of the inventory, he shall report it, without delay to the Inspector of Customs, who has the superintendence of all matters connected with the harbour and pdotage. $ 11. At the end of every year the head pilot shall deliver to the Inspector of Customs a list of all the appurtenances of the harbour, intended for the security of the shipping, together with the necessary information in reference to the condition they are in, as also a list of the rest of the inventory with similar elucidations. $ 12. Every transgression of these rules, remissness of the pilots in the performance of their duties, refractory conduct or disobedience of orders will be punished, unless otherwise directed by the above, either with a fine imposed by the Inspector of Customs or by the Government ; or, according to circumstances, with dismissal from service. In case of a transgression of a serious nature, it will depend upon the decision of the Government, whether the offender is instantly to be dismissed or to be arraigned. If the offence in question has caused the loss of any revenue, the fine imposed ought at least to equal the amount of the pilotage, which thus has been lost, and in case of dismissal the offender ought likewise to be compelled to make good the revenue thus lost. Which regulations, in conformity with the above Royal Resolution, are hereby put in force.

London Times. December 16, 1851. FRANCE. (from another correspondent.) Sunday. Although there is nothing in the general aspect of the city þÿ except the vast numbers of soldiers and ogens de police who inlest the streets in the day time, and the patrols of military, horse and fool, at the dead hours of night, telling dark tales of suspicion and arrest þÿ to suggest to the stranger that Paris is at the present time different ftom its ordinary self, there is no such thing as a feeling of confidence in the masses, nor can any Frenchman, much less foreigner, ts.keit upon himself to assert that he has a clear notion of the actual stale of affairs Resistance has been put down, or. rather, strangled in the cradle, not hy the strong arm of the law, for the law has been put aside as an empty pretence, but by the strong arm of a new dictator, on the eve of making a new law lo suit lus own purposes, and legalize, so io say, bis mteinpt for the old one. In this condition ol vagueness and uncertainty things will, in all probability, remain until the re-eleciion of Louis Napoleon, by "universal sullrage," for a term of ten years, to the Presidency of France shall have placed him in a position to act with some colour of authority, and to iav before the nation, bewildered and distracted by recent events, his ideas of a Constitution, and the means lie thinks the fittest to establish tranquility and general satisfaction on a solid basis. Meanwhile the formation of the Commission Consultative, of which the members' names were published some time since, has

been attended by numerous protestations on the part of persons who, without their consent being asked, have been announced as belonging to it. Among others, the Due d'.Vlbufera paid a visit to the Minister of the Interior, to complain of his name having been published without permission, and to request that it might be erased from the list. M. de Morny, however, is stated to have replied, with imperturbable coolness: þÿ "Monsieur nous avons besoin de voire nom; nous I'avons pris. Quant ii voire personne, nous.n'en avons quoi faire. Seolement je vous invite a vous lenir tranquille and turned upon his heel, to the astonishment of his stupefied auditor. Doubtless these reports are exaggerated, but if the substance of them be correct, of which I have very little doubt, what

St. <0 O I I£ ATI 3 becomes of the personal independence of a Fiench gentleman ? M. Joseph Perier, who was treated with the same want of ceremony, is reported to have gone about the streets with an instrument to erase bis name from the official announcement wherever it was posted. M. le Comte Beugnot, 1 am inloi tiled, had recourse to a more ingenious and original expedient. He ordered cartes de visile to be printed as follows þÿ " M. le Cotnte Beugnot, ex-represemant, mais non membre de la Commission Consultative" þÿ and caused them to be distributed among his friends and acquaintances. Others had recourse to circular letters. There is no doubt that a great many who have indignantly declined the honour of forming pai l of the Commission in question are deprived of the means of making their refusal and the motives tor it known to the public, (he press, being entirely at ihe mercy of the Government, not daring to make current any lads whatever thai might give umbrage lo the existing powers. It is not generally known that nearly thirty persons were kept under attest at the Cafe Tortoni on Thuisday, the 4th mst., although the military, who entered the house, could find nothing whatever lo justify their suspicion that shots had been tired trom it. Among these persons were M. Jaubert, Major in the Belgian Cavalry ; M. le Coniie Michel de Michelski (a Polish gentleman, as his name suggests), a Lieutenant-Colonel in the English army; Mr. E. A. Waller, civil engineer (an Englishman,) said to be an aide-dc-

camp of the Prince de Joinville; a number of other gentlemen, the waiters at the cale, and ttuee ladies. Although it was explained, and, indeed, was sufficiently evident, that the majority of these persons were at 'Bottom's for the simple purpose of taking some refreshment, and were dissuaded from leaving by the unusual aspect ol the Boulevards, they were taxed with being privy to the attack upon the soldiery (which, like most of the other so-called " attacks," has never been substantiated), kept under arrest at Tortom's until hail past 7 in the evening, and then mar died of), hi pairs, under escort (ladies and all) to the Tuileries, where, alter waiting more than an tiour in the outer yard, they were examined before nn officer, who, at once seeing the absurdity of Ihe charge, dismissed them all, except as 1 am told, by one who was present, the supposed aide-de-camp of the Prince de Joinville. All kinds of rumours are current about the new "Constitution" which Louis Napoleon is to draw up and submit to the Commission Consultative, of which M. Baroche is vicepresident. It has been affirmed, and in many quarters is believed, that there are to be three Chambers þÿ a Senate, a Council of State, and a Chamber of Legislation, the latter to consist of 300 members ; the members of the Senate to receive a salary of 36,000f., the members of the Council of Stale 24,000f. , and those of the Chamber of Legislation 12,000f., annually. The plan is riot a bad one to unite the interests of the legislators

with those of the President and his intimate allies. The duration of their þÿfunctions probably ten years, like the President's term of office þÿ would, however, render universal suffrage a by-word and a mockery long before the expiration of that period. It appears there is no cessation in the progress of arrest. On two occasions lately a number of persons were at rested at the Divan

Lepelletien who, upon expostulating, were asked for letters addressed to them as a proof"oi their identity. All, I am told, were enabled to produce the required documents, except one þÿ M Xavier Dtirieu, a late writer in the National þÿ und all, except that gentleman, were released. 1 have just been told that 400 prisoners were removed the day before yesterday from the Coneiergeriet whose further destination remains a mystery. Nearly all the papers have re appeared. The exceptions I have remarked are the National, the Avenement, the Semaine, the Keforme, the Democratic Pacifique, and the llepublique, the majority of which 1 believe, however, are not merely suspended, but suppressed. There aie no political leaders, or paragraphs, in any of them except in the Constitutionnel, the l'atrie, and the Pays, M. de la Guerroniere, in the last mentioned journal, offers a lengthened apology for having resumed his pen in favour of existing things þÿ under the head of " Pourquoi nous ecrivon«." M. Peroddeau, the new editor of the Presse, also puts forth a profession of faith, from which it may be galheted that his political opinions are not those of his predecessor, JV1 Girardin, I should have mentioned in my first letter, that, coming fiom London to Paris, the persons of many of the voyngeurs (especially "natives") were searched for papers, and that at all the chief stations between Calais and Paris soldiers appeared and anxiously scrutinized the occupants of every carriage

in the train, it was at this period that M. Louis Blanc and other refugies were reported to have started for Paris, besides the Prince de Juinville, whose appearance would possibly inspire apprehensions of a still more formidable nature. þÿ ooo»- St. Thomas Times, January 10, 1852.
