St. Thomas Times , January 14, 1852. Extensive l ire at Washington. Washinoton, Dec. 24, 1851. The Congressional Library was nearly destroyed by fire to-day, and the whole Capitol came very near being consumed. The fire was discovered at half-past seven o'clock this morning in the Library of Congress, try a watchman. The flames were first seen issuing front a table near the centre ol the room, and soon enveloped the shelving on the northwest side. A few buckets of water would then have suppressed the fire, hut before they could be procured the entire library was in flames. The smoke was so dense that the persons who rushed in were unable to save any of the contents, except four or five portraits of the Bresidents. The marble busts, and splendid cases one of them tastefully adorned and filled, with twelve hundred bronze medals presented by Vatlemere together with all splendid þÿ the works of art in the cases, were conswmed-

Tiie entire library contained upwards of f, 0,000 volumes, including the library of Jefferson, which formed the nuc.leus. All in the main room is lost. The books in an adjoining room (upwards of 20,000 including ihe law library), were saved. The total loss of hooks is variously estimated at between 8100 000 and 8250,000 ; but no money can replace many of the works thus destroyed. The roof of the library is all burned, and the exterior of the building, on the west, is blackened. The parapet wall has expanded, so as to render its removal necessaiy. At one time, such was the progress of the flames that the dome was in imminent dang'-r, as well as the roof of both houses. The dome and roofs are made of wood, coppered over, but lined inside with a composition of pitch, so as to render them waterproof. An engine was placed in the rotunda, and every passage was flooded with water. The greater part of the water was conveyed in buckets. The two Chambers of Congress nre uninjured, and business will not be arresicd. The utmost activity was exhibited by all classes of citizens, thousands of whom were in attendance. The marines stationed here were ordered out by government to repair to the spot, while the Mayor and other authorities personally exerted themselves- The whole force of the mechanics and marines belonging to the Navy Yard, worked incessantly till the flames were extinguished. The Bresident and members of the cabinet were on the ground all the morning, giving directions, and urging on the firemen and

workmen to almost superhuman exertion. We noticed prominently among the workers Senator Gwin passing the buckets along. The water had to he conveyed into the Capitol from the basins in the grounds, there being no reservoirs anywhere in the building itself. Owing to the dense volume of smoke, all attempts to save anything, when the fire was first discovered, were unavailing. The cold was intense, and the firemen suffered very much. The heat from the burning books in the library was overpowering ; hut the ceiling being fireproof, the roof was partly protected. it has not vet been ascertained how the fire originated. The library was heated by flues, and there having been no fire in the room for many years, the fire must either have communicated through the hot air flues, or been the work of an incendiary. Of course the whole matter will be thoroughly investigated. The flames were subdued by twelve o'clock. A guard of marines has been detained to watch during the night. A fire in the Franklin Hotel took place before daylight. The hoarders, and the family of Mr. Baker, escaped with difficulty. the latest relative to the hue. Washington, Dec. 24 þÿ 10 B. M. About sixty thousand volumes of the Library of Congress were destroyed, exceeding in value a quarter of a million of dollars þÿ Jefferson's library, for which Congress paid forty thousand dollars, wasenlirely consumed. Many of these hooks were highly valuable, þÿ on account of the marginal notes in Jefferson's handwriting. Hare hooks, (resented

The all-engrossing topic of the Presidential election was occupying the French mind, to the exclusion of all other matters. Louis Napoleon has been elected to the Presidency for ten years, by an overwhelming majority of votes. The poll of sixty eight departments, though incomplete, gave ' yes," 5 400 000 ; " no," only 000.000. A telegraphic despatch from Paris, Dec. 26th gives as the voles of 81 departments, of which 23 were complete, "yes," 0,011,000; ' no," 709,000. Many of the deputies had been set at liberty, and much speculation was indulged in as to the new press law to be shortly promulgated. The best informed persons think that each journal will have to deposit a certain sum with the government as security for good behavior. The offences of the press were to be, 1st, Attack upon the President ; 2d, Inciting hatred among citizens; 3d, An attack upon religion, family, or property. Each offence was to be punished by line and imprisonment. The correspondent of tiie London Globe, writing from Paris, on Friday morning, says, that amongst the rumors in Paris is one to the effect that seme ministerial changes will accompany or follow tfie assumption of the government when pronounced legal by the vote of the people. Munialcmbcrt is spoken of as likely to form part of the new cabinet, and that the portfolio of public instruction

will be confided to him ; but that M. M. llonder and Fould. and General St. Arnaud will remain in office. The papers stale that the police of Kenis, having been informed that some of the refugees in London were about to enter lii þÿit Admiral Dubourdieu and the Pasha of Tantanv from Jersey, measures were taken to arrest them. Three days back, M. Brochers, Commissary of Police, gave orders to arrest a young man who presented himself with a passport quite irregular. " You are," said M. Brochers, " furnished with a passport which is not worth anything. It is under a false name. Your own name is Le Balleaine de Villiers, son of t he editor of the Posciit. You are from London, and you have been teported several limes condemned for political offences " The young man was obliged to ndmit the truth of the magistrate's statement, and in an hour afterwards he was on his way, under escort, to Paris

The resignation of Lord Palmerston caused a temporary disarrangement of tfie various markets, and a decline of prices in many occurred þÿ but when it became known that Lord Granville was to succeed Lord Palmerston, confidence became in some measure restored. The sudden retirement of Lord Palmerston front the office of Foreign Secretary, caused the greatest amazement and most profound regret of the whole nation. His successor, it is officially announced, is Lord Granville. The withdrawal of Lord Palmerston from the government is imputed to the dissensions which have been known to exist in the cabi-

©at®ttsi net for several months past, and was, probably, precipitated by the significant reception and emphatic avowal of opinion to the Kossuth deputation, to whom his Lordship used language by no means complimentary to the absolutists of Europe. The fearless position assumed by his Lordship proved distasteful to the majority of the Ministry, and hence the result. This has been the all-prevailing topic of conversation at this festive season, and has created a universal sensation. The under-secretary Lord Stanley had also tendered his resignation. Among the rumored causes of Lord Palmerston's secession from the cabinet, was that of a diflerence of opinion upon the abstract question of the French revolution though the mystery is not likely to he revealed before the meeting of Parliament. It would appear that the return of many Irish emigrants to their own country, had attracted considerable attention in helund, as in very many instances, the expectations entertained had not been realized. The Irish were congratulating themselves upon it, and regarded it as a ground of hope. ; One of the members of an extensive drysaltery establishment in Liverpool, had ab- i sconded, after appropriating funds to the amount of £50,000. The liabilities are stated at £70 000 The house of Quarles. Ham & Sons, in the Oporto trade, has failed, with liabilities slated at £90,000.

| ment that AI. AIailefbrt's system should be tried on the rock of which we have been speaking : " It having been announced in the newspapers for tluee or lour days previous, that Al. proceeded to carry out his arrangements. Very interesting from Nicaragua San Juan de Nicaragua, ) Grey Town, December 5, 1851. j The Firing at the Prometheus þÿ Statement by American Citizens. The citizens of the United States residing in San Juan, or Grey town, deeming it necessary that a correct account of the lateaffair in the harbour of this place should be laid before the American people, respectfully request the publication in the Herald of the following statement: þÿ The port of San Juan del Norte, (Grey Town,) is a free port, all articles imported or exported are free of duty. The city government consists of a council, of which Mr. G reen. the English Consul, is chairman. The council is composed of five members, exclusive of the chairman, and are chosen annually by general election by the citizens. The names of the present council are Messrs Wm. Grey, II. L. Stevenson, A. Sigtmd, S. Shepherd, J. Geddus. Messrs. Grey and Stevenson are Americans, Mr. Siguad is a Frenchman, Mr. Shepherd is a native of this coast, and Mr Geddes is a native of Scotland. Each member of the Council is by right of office, a magistrate; and any act whatever relating to the city or the harbour, must be approved by the council before it can become a law. There is a regularly organised police for the maintenance of order, or a City Attorney to discharge the usual duties of that office, and a Port Captain and a. Port Surgeon, whose duty it is to board all vessels entering the harbor. All vessels entering the harbor are required to pay harbor dues, except the En-

glish mail steamers. These vessels are exempt because they bring and receive a mail to and from this place. The same privilege is afforded to the steamer of any other country that will in like manner deliver and receive a mail to and from the countries from which they come. The steamship Prometheus commenced her regular trips to this port in July last in connection, by the transit steamers on the river and lake, with the steamers from San Francisco at San Juan del Sur. The author i tics of this place granted to the company the privilege of occupying a certain portion of land on the opposite or north side of the harbor for the purpose of fitting up the river steamers, discharging coal &c. There ap. pcared to be a disposition, on the part of the government here, to render to the company such facilities as might be in their power in establishing the route ; and when the first steamer started on her first voyage up the river and grounded on a sand bar opposite the town, the boats of the war vessel Bermuda, then lying in port, were promptly sent to her relief, and assisted in getting her off. Previous to the departure of the Prometheus for New York, the bill for port charges was presented and pavmeut refused, on the plea that the company did not recognize the authorities, and consequently would not pay. This announcement was received with surprise and regret, as it was the wish of the authorities and citizens that a good understanding should exist between them and the

company. The Prometheus was permitted to depart, and made several trips, each time refusing to pay as before, at the same time all other vessels arriving and departing paid the regular charges without a murmur.

On the morniog of November 2 1 st, the Prometheus, then in port, and about to start for New York, with a large number of passengers, among them Mr. Vanderbilt. president the canal company, who had just returned from the lake Nicaragua, whither he had went with the new lake steamer Central America. The usual bill of charges was presented including those due on former occasions, and payment again refused. A warrant was then issued (the council approving) for the arrest of the Captain of the steamer for the debt. J he Captain of the port, with some policemen, went on board, and on serving the process, the captain of the steamer resisted ; on this the Port Captain, with his men, retired, at the same time giving notice that the steamer would not be permitted to proceed to sea until the debt was paid. In a few minutes alter, the Prometheus was dropping down the harbour, and immediately the English brig of-war Express, got under way. One or two blank cartridges were fired. The steamer still con tin ut d dropping down, a round shot was then sent across the bow, and another across the stern from the brig. The steamer then returned to her place of anchorage Mr. Vanderbill came on shore and the debt was paid. It is a matter of regret to the Americans residii g in Man Juan, t ha t such an occurience should have taken place. Nearly one-half the unproved property is held, and more than one half the business is done, by Americans. For good order and for safety of life and of

property, Grey Town will compare favorably with any town in any country, and while Chagres has established art unenviable reputation, and San Juan del Sur and Virgin Bav are following the same track, Grey Town or San Juan del Norte, presents the singular contrast of good order and safety, whilst almost surrounded by Spanish American anarchy. There seems an anomaly in the fact that while the Prometheus recognized no authority in Grey Town, they repeatedly called on the authorities to assist them in quelling insubordination on board their vessels. It is but a short time ago, that the Captain of the Prometheus applied directly to the Captain of the English brig-of-war in the harbor for assistance, on the event of a difficulty with his passengeis, which he expected would take place. The Americans here deem the Mosquitto question a matter to be settled between the governments interested; and until that is done, that in order to maintain the laws and give protection to citizens and strangers that the usual port chniges, as well as all other taxes levied by consent of the council, should be paid ; and it may be here added that I to the Roman Catholic Americans in buying property landed or otherwise, or accepting office under the government, are not required to relinquish a single right they may possess us American citizens. We the undersigned American merchants in Grey Town, certify the foregoing statement to be correct, and should it be necessary, you aie at liberty to use our names in
connection therewith. Respectfully, Henry L. Stephenson, P. F. Mnncoros, Wm. De Forest, Jos V. I'erez, Wm, Gray, Nick. Boilvin, Benjamin Clinton.

Origin of the Fenny Postage. A traveller sauntering through the lake districts of England some years ago arrived at a small public-house just, as the postman stopped to deliver a letter. A young girl came out to re-

it over and over, and asked the charge. no less than a shilling. Sighing heavily she observed that it came from her brother, but that she was too poor to take it in, and she returned it to the postman accordingly. The traveller was a man of kindby so much does the man ness as well as of observation ; he offered to pay the postage himself, and in spite of more reluctance on tiie girl's part than he could well understand, lie did pay it, and gave her the letter. JNo sooner, however, was the þÿpostman s back turned than she confessed that the proceeding had been concerted between her brother and herself; that, the letter was empty, that certain signs on the direction conveyed all that she wanted to know, and that, as they could neither of them afford to pay postage, they had devised this method of franking the intelligence desired. The traveller pursued his journey, and as he plodded over the Cumberland fells he mused upon the badness of a system which drove people to such straits for means of correspondence, and defeated its own all the such musing? would have ended before the close of the hour, but this þÿman s name was Hill, and it was from tin incident and the n reflections that the whole scheme of pennv postage w »derived.

Difficulty is a severe instructor, set over us by the supreme ordinance of a parental guardian and legislator, who knows us better than we know ourselves, and He loves us better too. He that wrestles with us, strengthens our nerves, and sharpens our skill. Our antagonist is our helper. This amicable ronllict with difficulty obliges us to an intimate acquaintance with our object, and compels us to consider it in ali ils relations. It will not suffer us to be superficial. A Horse Dealer was asked if an animal which lie offered for sale was timid. þÿ Not at þÿall, said lie; þÿ lie often passes many nights together by himself in the þÿstable. Riches do not consist in having more gold and silver, but in having more in proportion than our neighbors; whereby we are enabled to procure to ourselves ii greater plenty of the conveniences of life, than come within their reach, who, sharing the gold and silver of the world in a less proportion, want the means of plenty and power, and so arc poorer. We sometimes see a lool with wit, but never otic with judgment. If a man could have half his wishes, lie would double his troubles. We may, by afme education, learn to think most correctly, and talk most beautifully; but when it comes to action, if we are weak and undecided, w e are of all beings the most wretched. That þÿ is it not good for man to he þÿalone is true in more viewsofour species than one; and society gives strength to our reason a- well as polish to our manners. Manners rnak" a mat:.

St. Thomas: Times , January 24, 1852. Tin- only circumstance of a local character which has come to our knowledge during the present week is one of a truly heart-rending and melancholy nature. Yesterday morning the body of a fullgrown male infant, of very fair complexion, supposed to be several days old, was found wrapped in a chemise floating about one of the wharfs in this town. The remains of the poor innocent were picked up, placed in a box, and removed to the Hospital, where an examination was held over the body by the þÿKing sPhysician, but owing to us decomposed state, no decisive conclusion could be arrived at as to the cause of death. We are however of opinion that this is another þÿ a similar case having occurred some time about the month of October 1850 þÿ case of Infanticide, and we feel pity for the unlor lunate wretch who has been guilty of this inhuman þÿact, being sensible that although the efforts of man may prove insufficient to discover the murderer, yet the all-seeing eye of an over-ruling Providence has be'- n w itness to the horribly sinful act, and His arm will wield ihe Hod of Punishment in this case.

In consequence þÿof the non-arrival of the outward 2nd of January mails, the steamers Esk and Great Western have been despatched, the former at 0 p. m., on the 25th, for Barbados, &c.» and the latter at 8 a. m., this day, for Jamaica and Mexico, so as to convey the inter-colonial mails arid passengers, also to bring the return mails lor the steamers going homeward about the 5th and 20th February. We have made enquiry at the Compaþÿny s Office, and have been informed by Mr. Cameron, the Superintendent, that the following course may probably he adopted by him, should the outward steamer continue missing. The steamer Medway, Captain Hast, due here from Chagres about the Hist instant, may he coaled and despatched about the 2nd February to Chagres, &c., in time to embark there the homeward mails, specie, and passengers, at the proper date, namely, the liiii of February, þÿ returning to St. Thomas by the 17th, when she would coal, and take the mails homeward, in the place of the Amazon, thus preventing all disappointment. The steamer Conway, Captain Sawyer, due here about the 2nd February, from Honduras, would, in such case, receive all the home mails, &t\, from the Medway, and proceed home in place of the latter vessel, on arrival of the Derwent from Windward. The steamer Derwent, Captain W eller, may not be looked lor here, Irom Windward, before the 5th February, in consequence of the Fsk having only left this place, for Barbndoes, on the 25th instant, as mentioned above ;

and, should the Conway go home on the 5th February in place of the Medway, the Derwent would take up the Havana route, with the outward mails of the 17th January, and continue thereon. The Eagle, Captain Jellicoe, remains in this harbour, being a spare ship; and should the Derwent proceed on the Honduras route, about the 6th or 7th February, the Eagle will receive the outward 17th January mails, and carry them to Barbados, Trinidad, &c., afterwards continuing on such route. The Fsk, Captain Restarrick, will remain at Barbados till the arrival of the 17th January out mails, to convey them to Demerara, and will continue performing that service until the arrival of another ship in place of the outward missing steamer. It will thus be seen, that, the non-arrival of the Amazon will cause no interruption to the þÿCompany s mail service homeward, or inter-colonially, the disappointment of not receiving the outward mail of the 17th January until late being the only drawback. The þÿCompany Superintendent s here is of opinion t hat the Amazon must have left Southampton on the 2nd January, and afterwards damaged some important part of the new machinery, in which case she would, no doubt, immediately make the best of her way back to the nearest safe port in the English Channel ; and if she could not accomplish this before the J 7th Jan., we may not hear anything of her by even the next outward steamer, which wili probably be the Dee, due here about the 7 1 h Feb.; however we

hope to have our anxiety set at rest, by the arrival of either a special steamer sent out, or the Dee. The Master of the þÿCompany coal s ship resources to be the þÿ sugarbarrel." þÿ Jeanette, which left Newport on the 30th December, and arrived here on '

fhe 20th instant, was informed before leaving, that the Amazon was the ship appointed to leave Sothampton on the 2nd January with the mails for 1lu> West Indies; and he also reports that the weather generally all the vva\ across was most favorable. He adds, that on the 20th January, in latitude North 19.35, and longitude West If, a large steamer passed him, about eleven a. m., steering for the Westward, namely, towards the passage between Antigua and Guadeloupe. Hie was about 3 miles from the Jeanette, ! ul showed no colours, and was steaming along, with all canvass set, at the rate of about It knots an hour. The steamer had one tunnel and two masts, and was square rigged on the foremast only. Now, the Amazon has two funnels and three masts, therefore it could not he that ship. It was at first thought that possibly the Teviot, with two masts, might either have started on the 2nd January, with the outward mails, or afterwards on hearing ol the Amazon being broken down ; but if this had been tincase, and the Teviot iuul even gone into Antigua for coals, she would have been here by the 25th or 2(ith in þÿstunt, consequently, the steamer seen could not have been even the Teviot, except some accident has happened to her since the 20th instant, which is not very possible. þÿ St. Thomas Times , Jura ary 28.

At this time another boat was seen, supposed to he the gig, riding like the lifeboat, head to sea, but was not afterwards seen by those in the life-boat. The steamer was at this lime in a complete blaze fore and aft, and about 5 30 a. rn. her magazine blew up, and in less than a quarter of an hour

At daylight there was a heavy fall of rain, which lessened the sea, and the boat, which had then drifted about three miles from where the Amazon went down, after searching for any portion of the wre ok, and finding no vessel in sight, was put before the wind, and continued pulling towards the eastward, with five oars aside till noon, when they descried a vesset about three miles to windward, on the starboard tack, standing to the southward; they hoisted signals and pulled towards her, and the brig perceiving them bore down. The Dutch vessel Gertruida, Tuntelcr, entered the roads here to-day with 25 shipwrecked persons, picked up in two boats from tne Amazon. SSlie picked up the first boat yesterday (Sunday, the 4th of January), at half-past six þÿo clock in the evening, and the second this morning at seven þÿo clock. In the presence of such a catastrophe, the British vice-consul, in the absence of Sir Anthony Perrier, the consul, w ho is detained in Paris by his duties as a member of the International Sanatory Commission, lost no time in endeavouring to save tiie lives of those who, according to the accounts given by the passengers who have arrived here, were saved in the four or five other boats which escaped from the wreck, and which, from all appearance, must still be struggling against the waves. The maritime prefect was immediately applied to, nii he at once agreed to give every assistance, and the SoulHcur steamer, which was in the harbour, was immediately ordered out.
